title: The Letter from Denia. The old epistle of Ibn Gharsiya, a Basque Christian taken as a child and raised a Muslim at the court of Denia, passes from hand to hand among the secretaries: the Arabs, he wrote, are masters at describing camels, and philosophy, astronomy and the measuring of the earth belong to the peoples they conquered. The court answers that a man is what he knows

data.text: the quarrel is an old one in al-Andalus: Berbers carried the conquest, Slavs commanded the palace guard and the sons of converted natives filled the chanceries, yet the old Arab families still count a man's descent before they count his learning; a realm that means to hold the whole peninsula cannot afford the habit (the game's text)
data.choice: A man is what he knows (the only option shown)

title: The integration of the Ṭāʾifa of Balansiyya into the crown is nearly complete, and the court prepares to accept the Catalans on the same standing as the Portuguese. The Castilians are left out, ignored at best

data.valencia: annexation of the ṭāʾifa nearly complete (Trent)

title: The Emperor orders a great road built from Ishbīliya to Balansiyya. Once the ṭāʾifa is integrated, a governor will sit at Balansiyya to carry the empire's influence into the Mediterranean. It is also a military road, to move the armies quickly toward the French border should another crusade be preached

data.purpose: a governor's seat at Balansiyya, to project influence into the Mediterranean (Trent)
data.date: April 1419, after the Letter from Denia (Trent's account gives no exact day)
data.military: a road for moving troops to the French border in case of another crusade (Trent)
